{{Short description|Genus of extinct bird}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = Middle [[Eocene]]
([[Lutetian]]), ~{{fossilrange|47.2}} | image = Masillastrix blattophaga (holotype, SMF-ME 11964).jpg | image_caption = Holotype under different preparation stages, including stomach contents in inset (A) | display_parents = 2 | genus = Masillastrix | parent_authority = [[Gerald Mayr|Mayr]] ''in'' Mayr et al., [[2026 in paleontology|2026]] | species = blattophaga | authority = Mayr ''in'' Mayr et al., 2026 }} '''''Masillastrix''''' ({{lit|Messel owl}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[Stem group|stem]]-[[owl]] known from the mid-[[Eocene]] ([[Lutetian]] age) [[Messel Pit]] of Germany. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Masillastrix blattophaga''''', known from a nearly complete [[postcrania]]l skeleton preserved on a [[Compression fossil|slab and counterslab]]. This specimen is the first owl fossil with well-preserved feathers from the tail and wings. ''Masillastrix'' is the second owl fossil described from the Messel Pit, following ''[[Palaeoglaux artophoron]]''. The preserved stomach contents of the ''Masillastrix'' specimen reveal an [[iridescent]] [[cockroach]], representing both the first instance of an insect as a fossil bird's last meal and the only known instance of an owl—extinct or otherwise—preying on this type of cockroach. == Discovery and naming == The ''Masillastrix'' fossil material was discovered by Bruno Behr during an excavation in 2025 at outcrops of the [[Messel Formation]] near in [[Messel]], [[Darmstadt-Dieburg]], Germany. The specimen was taken to the [[Naturmuseum Senckenberg|Senckenberg Research Institute]] in [[Frankfurt]], where Behr [[Fossil preparation|prepared]] it, and it is now permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen SMF-ME 11964. It consists of a nearly complete skeleton missing most of the skull and the tip of the left forelimb, flattened on two opposing [[Compression fossil|slabs]], designated as A and B. Extensive feather traces are preserved around the wings and tail, the first such occurrence in a fossil owl. In 2026, [[Gerald Mayr]] and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Masillastrix blattophaga'' as a new genus and species of early owl based on these fossil remains, designating SMF-ME 11964 as the [[holotype]] specimen. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Masillastrix'', combines the [[Latin]] name for Messel, {{lang|la|Masilla}}, with the Latin {{lang|la|[[:wikt:strix#Latin|strī̆x]]}}, meaning {{gloss|owl}} (also the genus name of [[Strix (bird)|earless owls]]). The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''blattophaga'', derives from ''[[Blatta]]'', a cockroach genus, and the [[Greek language|Greek]] word {{lang|grc|[[:wikt:φᾰγεῖν|φᾰγεῖν]]}} ({{lang|grc|phăgeîn}}), meaning {{gloss|to eat}}. ''Masillastrix'' is the second fossil owl named from the Messel Pit, following ''[[Palaeoglaux artophoron]]'' in 1992. == References == {{Cite journal |last1=Mayr |first1=Gerald |last2=Šmídová |first2=Lucia |last3=Richter |first3=Adrian |last4=Wedmann |first4=Sonja |date=2026-11-02 |title=Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl |journal=[[Current Biology]] |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079 |doi-access=free}} {{Cite book |last1=Peters |first1=Dieter Stefan |title=Papers in avian paleontology honoring Pierce Brodkorb |publisher=No. 36 Science Series, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County |year=1992 |editor-last=Campbell, Jr. |editor-first=Kenneth E. |pages=161–169 |chapter=A new species of owl (Aves: Strigiformes) from the Middle Eocene Messel oil shale |issn=((0079-0943)) |chapter-url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/348547#page/203/mode/1up |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/217605}} {{Strigiformes|S.|state=collapsed}} {{Taxonbar|from1=Q141984174|from2=Q141984177}} [[Category:Owls]] [[Category:Eocene birds of Europe]] [[Category:Extinct birds of Europe]] [[Category:Monotypic prehistoric bird genera]] [[Category:Fossil taxa described in 2026]] [[Category:Taxa named by Gerald Mayr]]
